title: Detect an override when @Override is gone

blocks.text: `@Override` has SOURCE retention: the compiler checks it and then throws it away, so `method.isAnnotationPresent(Override.class)` is always `false`. The page's answer (Q4) is to inspect the class hierarchy instead, and warns that its own snippet looks only at the direct superclass.

Write `Overrides.isOverride(Method m)`. It returns `true` when `m` is neither `static` nor `private` and a **supertype** of its declaring class declares a method that is neither `static` nor `private`, with the same name **and the same parameter types**. Supertypes are **every superclass up to `Object`** and every interface reached from them, directly or through other interfaces; their abstract and default methods both count. A `private` method in a supertype is not overridden.

cases.says: Dog.speak() is an override although reflection cannot see its @Override, and Dog.fetch() is not.
Dog.speak(String) and Dog.equals(Dog) share a name with a supertype method but not its parameter types, so they are not overrides.
Dog.toString() overrides Object.toString() although Animal, the direct superclass, does not declare it.
A class's greet(String) and wave() implement an abstract and a default method of an interface it reaches directly or through another interface.
Dog.secret() has the signature of Animal's private secret(), which no subclass can override.

origin.section: Common Pitfalls and How to Avoid Them

concepts: @Override has SOURCE retention, so reflection never sees it and an override is found by searching the supertypes for the same signature.
Without @Override a typo or a wrong parameter type, such as equals(Dog), silently declares a new method instead of overriding.
